messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Even in these lines, Majeed’s cunning and apathy are not absent; they are masked by action. His command, “Wake up, Bibi,” sounds protective, yet he is the one carrying Jamila, leading bewildered Rahima, and exploiting the moonlit moment. That is controlled, strategic behavior, not spontaneous mercy.

If the rescue were deontological, it would rest on duty: he acts because saving his family is right in itself. The text allows a flicker of that sense of responsibility, but it does not prove pure good-will. More persuasive is a teleological reading: he moves them because the result is useful to him. It removes them from the house, protects his image, and lets him direct the scene. Thus the lines show a hybrid: duty is performed, but the action is better understood as well-calculated.

Palindromes:
radar
level
rotor
kayak
madam
civic
refer
stats
deified
repaper
